Disability-income planning: fund the waiting period and the months after payments end

Four graphics map temporary pay, a delayed net insurance benefit, payment duration and the cash reserve needed across an income interruption.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 4 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Hypothetical month-end household cash ledger. Temporary salary/sick-pay receipts arrive in the initial selected months. Insurance first pays after the full selected waiting months and then pays for the selected number of months, limited by the illustrated horizon. Benefit input is assumed approved and available after all taxes and offsets; the model does not apply coordination rules. Continuing income, temporary pay and net insurance receipts are added as entered, including any overlap. Setup cost is paid at time zero. No interest, inflation, claim assessment, medical eligibility, premium, statutory benefit, recovery date or administrative delay is calculated. Negative cash positions represent unfunded needs, not an approved loan.

The central idea

A monthly benefit amount tells only part of the story. Put the first receipt, overlapping income and the final modeled payment on a calendar before assessing the cash reserve.

01

Read the contract, then build the cash calendar

The Financial Consumer Agency of Canada’s disability-insurance guide highlights waiting times, benefit amounts, tax treatment, definitions of disability and coordination with other benefits. Those details affect both eligibility and the cash a household can use. A policy’s headline payment should not automatically be treated as additional net income.

This illustration assumes a selected benefit is approved and available after all taxes and offsets. It does not assess a claim or determine an entitlement. Continuing household income, temporary salary or sick pay, and the entered net insurance benefit are separate receipts in a monthly ledger.

The waiting input counts full months with no insurance receipt. A three-month wait means the first modeled payment arrives at the end of month four. The payment-count input then specifies how many monthly receipts occur within the selected horizon. These are hypothetical timing assumptions, rather than a policy quotation or a prediction of recovery.

02

The income gap can change more than once

The default household spends CAD 4,500 each month and retains CAD 1,500 of continuing net income. Temporary salary or sick pay adds CAD 2,500 in each of the first two months. The remaining monthly gap is CAD 500 while that temporary payment is present.

In month three, the temporary receipt has ended but insurance has not yet begun. The gap rises to CAD 3,000. In months four through nine, the entered CAD 2,200 insurance payment brings total net receipts to CAD 3,700, leaving CAD 800 a month to fund from cash.

The six modeled insurance payments then finish. Months ten through twelve again have a CAD 3,000 monthly gap. The first graphic makes these phases visible. It does not assume that a policy necessarily stops after six payments; that count is an editable stress scenario for the example.

03

Fund the deepest cash need, including the starting cost

The example also includes CAD 1,000 of one-time costs before the first month. From CAD 10,000 allocated cash, the starting position after that payment is CAD 9,000. The reserve then pays each monthly difference between receipts and spending.

Across the twelve-month schedule, the monthly gaps total CAD 17,800. Adding the initial CAD 1,000 gives a required starting amount of CAD 18,800. After the CAD 10,000 reserve already entered, another CAD 8,800 is needed under these assumptions.

The path first goes negative in month ten. A negative point is an unfunded requirement, not a bank balance the household is allowed to maintain. The second cash curve removes insurance receipts while keeping everything else the same, providing a no-receipt stress comparison without assigning it a probability.

04

Check overlaps and avoid counting the same support twice

The income-source bars sum only receipts inside the selected horizon. The default totals are CAD 18,000 of continuing income, CAD 5,000 of temporary pay and CAD 13,200 of entered insurance benefits. Amounts scheduled after the horizon do not appear in those totals.

The calculator adds inputs as entered. If temporary pay overlaps the insurance phase, the model does not reduce either amount automatically. Actual coordination needs to be resolved before using the figures: a payment already included in continuing income must not also be entered as a separate benefit.

Use amounts available for household bills after the relevant deductions and offsets. A gross insurance amount or an expected reimbursement can differ from spendable cash on the date a bill arrives. This model calculates neither tax nor the contractual treatment of another source of support.

05

Review waiting time, payment duration and the wider interruption

The matrix varies full waiting months and the number of insurance payments. Each cell is additional starting cash after the selected reserve, calculated across the same household schedule. Temporary pay, ongoing income, spending and the initial cost remain unchanged.

A longer wait and a shorter payment period affect different parts of the calendar. If payments begin after the illustrated horizon, none is counted. If income exceeds spending in a month, the surplus remains in the modeled cash reserve; the starting-cost requirement still exists before those receipts arrive.

The schedule excludes inflation, interest, claim administration, premiums and changes in spending or work capacity. Replace the assumptions with supported dates and net amounts when reviewing an actual arrangement. The useful output is a dated cash requirement alongside the coverage terms, rather than a conclusion that a headline replacement percentage makes every month affordable.
